summary: 15 concise trial-paper-only hypotheses distilled from the ResearchAgent run for sprint, grouped by per-hypothesis feature attribution.

mechanisms.description: Elevated urine NGAL normalized to creatinine measured at 3–7 days after intensification reflects acute tubular injury that predisposes to persistent eGFR loss rather than a benign hemodynamic decline.
An isolated early rise in plasma renin and aldosterone with absent urinary tubular injury markers indicates RAAS/volume‑mediated functional GFR reduction that is likely reversible by 3 months.
Persistent elevation of urine KIM‑1 and IL‑18 at 2–4 weeks identifies ongoing tubular injury that mediates progression to sustained eGFR decline and ESRD.
A predefined multimarker pattern combining high uNGAL/Cr and elevated uACR distinguishes an intrinsic kidney‑injury phenotype from isolated hemodynamic eGFR reductions.
Early decliners whose urinary injury markers remain low and whose hemodynamic panel reflects volume changes will predominantly experience reversible eGFR recovery by 3 months.
Biomarker‑positive findings in the early serial panel will correlate with measured‑GFR declines in the mGFR substudy, validating that biomarker elevation represents true loss of filtration.

Initiation or uptitration of ACEi/ARB without concomitant early biomarker elevation produces a hemodynamic, reversible eGFR fall, whereas concurrent biomarker elevation reflects maladaptive intrinsic injury.
Rapid normalization of tubular biomarkers between the 3–7 day and 2–4 week samples characterizes transient tubular stress from hemodynamic change and predicts eGFR reversibility.

An early multimarker score that is elevated despite modest creatinine‑based eGFR change captures noncreatinine injury pathways and independently identifies patients at higher risk for 3–5 year renal events.

A hemodynamic signature of elevated renin with low aldosterone and absent urinary injury markers denotes volume‑depletion‑mediated GFR fall that is mechanistically distinct from tubular injury and likely reversible.
Concordant increases in plasma cystatin C and creatinine during the early window indicate true filtration loss rather than a creatinine artifact, marking higher risk for long‑term renal events.

Intercurrent symptomatic hypotension or large BP variability together with rising tubular injury biomarkers indicates repeated hemodynamic insults that convert functional declines into structural kidney injury.
Higher baseline uACR predisposes to amplified early biomarker responses after intensive SBP lowering, reflecting limited renal reserve and greater likelihood of persistent eGFR loss.
An early increase in urine albumin‑creatinine ratio (uACR) after intensification signifies new or worsening glomerular permeability and predicts persistent eGFR decline.
Elevated NT‑proBNP together with increasing uACR after intensification suggests cardiorenal hemodynamic congestion that contributes to glomerular injury and persistent renal decline.
